title: Earthen vessels (2 Corinthians 4:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kentron, the sting Paul asked death about, and gave thanks for the victory. Who did you hold in mind? Day five hundred seventy-seven.

In the winter of 1946 to 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd threw a stone into a cave above the Dead Sea and heard something break. Inside were tall clay jars, and inside the jars, rolled scrolls: some of the oldest copies of the Hebrew scriptures ever found. Plain pots, the kind any household had, had kept them safe for nearly two thousand years. Paul never saw those jars. But writing to Corinth, he reached for the same picture to describe himself and every Christian: treasure, kept in clay.
screen: `A STONE THROWN INTO A CAVE.` → `SCROLLS IN PLAIN CLAY JARS.` → `TREASURE, KEPT IN CLAY.`

segments.voice: Just before today's verse, Paul has been talking about light. The God who said, let light shine out of darkness, he writes, has shone in our hearts. Then he says what holds that light: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us." The Greek word for earthen means plain baked clay, the stuff of ordinary pots and cheap oil lamps. Corinth made clay lamps by the thousand, and some scholars think Paul has a lamp in mind: a cheap clay shell with a flame inside. Why would God choose clay? Paul answers in the same verse: so that it's obvious where the power comes from. The Corinthians were impressed by polished speakers, and some of them found Paul unimpressive. His answer is not to polish himself up. It's to point at the cracks. In the next lines he lists them: pressed on every side but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. The clay takes the blows. The treasure stays. Catholics hear something of their own teaching here. The Church holds that the sacraments don't depend on the holiness of the priest who celebrates them: Christ acts in them, through the minister. The priest is clay. So is every bishop, every parent teaching a child the sign of the cross, every tired volunteer. That's not an excuse for carelessness. It's a kind of relief: the treasure was never theirs to begin with.
screen: `LIGHT OUT OF DARKNESS.` · `EARTHEN: PLAIN BAKED CLAY.` · `PRESSED, BUT NOT CRUSHED.` · `THE SACRAMENTS DON'T DEPEND ON THE PRIEST.` · then, large: `WE HAVE THIS TREASURE IN EARTHEN VESSELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a clay cup. If you can, pick up a mug or a ceramic bowl. If not, cup your empty hands as if you were holding one. Settle, and breathe. Feel its weight, the rough base, maybe a chip on the rim you've stopped noticing. Hold it gently, the way you'd hold something that could break. Then think of yourself the same way: breakable, and carrying something. If you pray, you can thank God for what you carry. If you don't, simply notice what you're holding and how carefully you hold it. The bell holds the time.
Earthen vessels. Paul's picture of himself and every Christian: plain clay jars, carrying a treasure that isn't their own. Today's word.
Your line: treasure in clay. Today, when you notice a crack in yourself, a bad mood, a failure, a tired body, remember the clay jars that kept the scrolls. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that the sacraments act by the power of Christ, not by the worthiness of the minister (ex opere operato), which is often explained with this verse in mind.

original.note: Greek: made of baked clay. from ostrakon, a potsherd, the same root as English 'ostracize'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic way of saying people are fragile.
what it means: God puts his treasure in plain clay on purpose, so the power is clearly his.
what a scholar hears: ostrakinos, baked clay, the stuff of cheap lamps, right after a verse about light shining out of darkness.

sources.quoted: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us.

notes: Dead Sea Scrolls: first cave found by Bedouin shepherds, winter 1946–47, scrolls in clay jars. Confirm details.
Corinthian clay lamp production and the suggestion that Paul has a lamp in mind: a scholarly suggestion, stated as such. Confirm.
Ex opere operato, CCC 1128; CCC 1584 on the unworthiness of the minister not preventing Christ from acting. Confirm.
Greek ostrakinos and the ostrakon/ostracism link: standard. Confirm.
